record.original_question: Does every triangulation of a surface by a complete graph admit a Grünbaum colouring?

evidence.quote: Question 5.4 Does every triangulation of a surface by a complete graph have a Grünbaum colouring?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $S$ be a closed surface (orientable or non-orientable) and let $G$ be a triangulation of $S$, meaning that $G$ is a simple graph embedded in $S$ so that every face of the embedding is bounded by a 3-cycle. A Grünbaum colouring of $G$ is an assignment of one of three colours to each edge of $G$ such that, for every face, the three edges on its boundary receive three distinct colours.

Suppose further that $G$ is isomorphic to a complete graph $K_n$ for some $n \ge 4$, i.e.\ the underlying graph of the triangulation is complete. 

Question: Does every such triangulation of a surface whose underlying graph is a complete graph admit a Grünbaum colouring?
artifact.status_search_result: The general question is not resolved in the literature found. Partial results exist: every triangulation of the sphere admits a Grünbaum colouring (equivalent to the Four Colour Theorem), and for complete graphs $K_p$ with $p \equiv 3, 7 \pmod{12}$ there exist orientable triangulations admitting a Grünbaum colouring. However, no source establishes the result for all complete-graph triangulations of all surfaces, and the problem appears to remain open.

status_evidence.title: Grünbaum coloring and its generalization to arbitrary surfaces
status_evidence.snippet: For each p ≡ 3 or 7 (mod 12), there exists a Grünbaum colorable orientable 2-dimensional triangulation by the complete graph Kp.
status_evidence.claim: Partial positive result for complete graphs Kp with p ≡ 3, 7 (mod 12); general question not settled.

status_evidence.title: Grünbaum colorings of even triangulations on surfaces
status_evidence.snippet: Even triangulations with no Grünbaum coloring exist with representativity 1, 2, 3 for all but finitely many surfaces.
status_evidence.claim: Grünbaum colourings do not always exist for general triangulations of surfaces, motivating the restricted complete-graph question.
